concept.name: Noncommercial trader
concept.definition: In the CFTC's legacy Commitments of Traders report, a reportable trader who does not qualify as commercial — encompassing professional money managers such as CTAs, CPOs, and hedge funds as well as a wide array of other non-commercial (speculative) traders. In the Disaggregated COT this group is split into Managed Money and Other Reportables.
concept.intuition: Noncommercials are the market's risk-takers: participants trading futures for profit rather than to hedge a physical business.
concept.mechanics: Classification is by CFTC staff judgment using Form 40 and other data, based on predominant activity. The legacy report shows noncommercial open interest long, short, and spreading, where spreading is the computed amount of offsetting long and short positions held by the same trader in different calendar months.
concept.failure_modes: The category is a residual mix — trend-following CTAs, discretionary macro funds, and other speculators are lumped together, so aggregate 'speculative' positioning can hide offsetting sub-currents. Classification involves judgment and can change over time, breaking continuity in historical series.
concept.misconceptions: Noncommercial does not mean retail or uninformed — most are professional managers; nor does a large noncommercial net position reliably mark tops or bottoms, since trends can extend positioning far beyond historical extremes.
concept.example: A CTA running a trend-following program builds a net long of 50,000 crude oil contracts; these appear in the legacy COT as noncommercial longs, and in the Disaggregated COT as managed money.
